Introduction
?

One type of indirect proof is the so-called proof by contrapositive. The method is based on the fact that the implication is logically equivalent to its contrapositive So, instead of proving the statement directly, we can instead prove its contrapositive form.

The outline of a typical contrapositive proof is the following:

Statement. If then

Proof.

Since we'll prove the contrapositive

Assumption: Suppose

Explanation of what means using axioms, definitions, or other results.

Algebraic techniques, logic, and further definitions or axioms are used to demonstrate, through a series of inferences, that implies

Conclusion: Therefore, So, since by the contrapositive

In many cases, proving the contrapositive form of a statement is easier than proving the original statement. In this lesson, we'll learn how to prove parity statements using the contrapositive.

Recall the following:

  • If an integer n is odd, then there exists an integer q such that n=2q+1.

n3−1 is even⇒n is odd

To prove P⇒Q, it suffices to prove the contrapositive ¬Q⇒¬P.

The contrapositive form of the given statement is n is not odd⇒n3−1 is not even which is equivalent to n is even⇒n3−1 is odd.

We start by using the fact that n is even.

If n is even, then n=2a, where a is an integer.

The idea is to substitute n=2a into the expression n3−1 and show it is odd by writing it as one more than a multiple of 2.

Substituting n=2a into the expression n3−1, we can show that n3−1=2b+1, where b is an integer.

Once we've done this, the proof is complete, and we can state our conclusion.

Therefore, since n3−1 is one more than a multiple of 2, we conclude that n3−1 is odd.
